title: Intrinsic carrier concentration and the mass-action law

sections.heading: The idea
sections.body_md:
In pure silicon, bonds are constantly breaking (generation) and electrons and holes are constantly meeting and re-forming bonds (recombination). In equilibrium the two rates balance. Generation depends only on temperature; recombination is proportional to how often an electron meets a hole, which goes as \(n\,p\). So the product \(n\,p\) is fixed by temperature alone. This is the **mass-action law**, and it remains true even after doping.

The intrinsic concentration grows very steeply with temperature because breaking a bond needs the bandgap energy: \(n_i\) roughly doubles every 8–11 K near room temperature.

sections.heading: Key equations
sections.body_md:
\[ n_0\,p_0 = n_i^2 \quad\text{(equilibrium)} \]
\[ n_i \propto T^{3/2}\,e^{-E_g/2kT} \]
Values used in this course at 300 K: \(n_i = 10^{10}\ \mathrm{cm^{-3}}\), \(n_i^2 = 10^{20}\ \mathrm{cm^{-6}}\), \(kT/q = 26\ \mathrm{mV}\), \(kT \approx 0.026\ \mathrm{eV}\).

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.body_md:
If a sample at 300 K somehow has \(n_0 = 4\times10^{12}\ \mathrm{cm^{-3}}\), the hole concentration must be
\[ p_0 = \frac{n_i^2}{n_0} = \frac{10^{20}}{4\times10^{12}} = 2.5\times10^{7}\ \mathrm{cm^{-3}} \]
Raising \(n\) by 400× lowered \(p\) by 400×. The exponent in \(n_i\) uses \(E_g/2kT\), not \(E_g/kT\), because each broken bond yields one carrier of each type.

sections.heading: Common pitfalls
sections.body_md:
- Using \(E_g/kT\) instead of \(E_g/2kT\) in the exponent.
- Applying \(np = n_i^2\) out of equilibrium, for example under illumination or bias.
- Forgetting to square \(n_i\).
- Plugging in temperature in °C. Use kelvin.

sections.heading: Where this leads
sections.body_md: The mass-action law is the tool you use to find the minority concentration in every doped region. It feeds directly into diode saturation current, which is proportional to \(n_i^2\) and therefore very temperature sensitive. Remember that the mass-action law holds only in equilibrium, which is why diodes and illuminated samples need the excess-carrier treatment later on.
